# From Euclidean Vectors to Vector Spaces

- [The previous deck found directions inside solution sets](#the-previous-deck-found-directions-inside-solution-sets)
- [A vector space starts with objects and two operations](#a-vector-space-starts-with-objects-and-two-operations)
- [The axioms force familiar consequences](#the-axioms-force-familiar-consequences)

## The previous deck found directions inside solution sets {#the-previous-deck-found-directions-inside-solution-sets}

As [{{< meta decks.d01.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#read-the-solution-set) showed,
elimination reveals free variables in a consistent system
$\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$

Choose one particular solution $\vct{x}_p$, so $\mat{A}\vct{x}_p=\vct{b}$

As [{{< meta decks.d05.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d05.file >}}#nonhomogeneous-systems-translate-those-directions) showed, all solutions have the form

$$
\{\text{all solutions}\}
=\vct{x}_p+\{\vct{z}:\mat{A}\vct{z}=\vct{0}\}
$$

The homogeneous solutions can be

- added to one another
- multiplied by scalars
- added to $\vct{x}_p$ without leaving the nonhomogeneous solution set

::: {.key-point}
This deck names the abstract structure shared by collections with these linear
operations
:::

## A vector space starts with objects and two operations {#a-vector-space-starts-with-objects-and-two-operations}

A [real vector space]{.alert} is a nonempty set $V$ whose elements are called
[vectors]{.alert}, with addition and multiplication by elements of $\reals$,
called [scalars]{.alert}:

$$
\vct{u}+\vct{v}\in V,
\qquad
c\vct{v}\in V
\qquad
(\vct{u},\vct{v}\in V,\ c\in\reals)
$$

These operations obey the vector-space axioms on the next two slides

::: {.key-point}
We specify the set and operations so polynomials, functions, and other objects
can be vectors, not only columns in $\reals^n$
:::

---

### Addition must behave like familiar vector addition {#addition-must-behave-like-familiar-vector-addition}

For all $\vct{u},\vct{v},\vct{w}\in V$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vct{u}+\vct{v}&\in V &&\text{closure}\\
\vct{u}+\vct{v}&=\vct{v}+\vct{u} &&\text{commutativity}\\
(\vct{u}+\vct{v})+\vct{w}&=\vct{u}+(\vct{v}+\vct{w}) &&\text{associativity}\\
\vct{v}+\vct{0}&=\vct{v} &&\text{zero vector}\\
\vct{v}+(-\vct{v})&=\vct{0} &&\text{additive inverse}
\end{aligned}
$$

The symbol $\vct{0}$ means the zero element of this particular space

---

### Scalar multiplication must fit addition {#scalar-multiplication-must-fit-addition}

For all $c,d\in\reals$ and $\vct{u},\vct{v}\in V$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
c\vct{v}&\in V &&\text{closure}\\
c(\vct{u}+\vct{v})&=c\vct{u}+c\vct{v}\\
(c+d)\vct{v}&=c\vct{v}+d\vct{v}\\
c(d\vct{v})&=(cd)\vct{v}\\
1\vct{v}&=\vct{v}
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Linear algebra uses only addition, scalar multiplication, and consequences of
these rules
:::

---

## The axioms force familiar consequences {#the-axioms-force-familiar-consequences}

Every vector space satisfies

$$
0\vct{v}=\vct{0},
\qquad
c\vct{0}=\vct{0},
\qquad
(-1)\vct{v}=-\vct{v}
$$

Let $\vct{w}=0\vct{v}$. Since $0+0=0$ for scalars, distributivity gives

$$
\vct{w}=(0+0)\vct{v}=\vct{w}+\vct{w}
$$

The additive-inverse axiom supplies $-\vct{w}$. Adding it to both sides gives
$\vct{0}=\vct{w}=0\vct{v}$

::: {.key-point}
Once the axioms hold, familiar algebraic manipulations work for every kind of
vector
:::

## Vectors need not be coordinate columns {#vectors-need-not-be-coordinate-columns}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
<h3>Familiar examples</h3>

- $\reals^n$
- complex vectors $\mathbb{C}^n$ with complex scalars
- geometric displacement vectors
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
<h3>New examples</h3>

- $m\times n$ matrices
- polynomials
- functions on an interval
- sequences
:::
:::

Addition and scalar multiplication are defined object by object

::: {.key-point}
Different objects can obey the same linear rules
:::

---

## The scalar field can change {#the-scalar-field-can-change}

Most of this course uses real scalars, but the same axioms work over any field

In the two-element field

$$
\mathbb{F}_2=\{0,1\},
\qquad
1+1=0
$$

Addition in $\mathbb{F}_2$ is [exclusive OR (XOR)]{.alert} on bits, familiar
from computer science

A vector in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ is a binary string; vector addition applies XOR
coordinatewise

For example,

$$
[1,0,1,1]^{\mathsf T}+[1,1,0,1]^{\mathsf T}=[0,1,1,0]^{\mathsf T}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Changing the scalar field changes which linear combinations are possible
:::

::: {.notes}
This compact extension beyond Anton's real-vector-space treatment provides a
natural connection to binary linear codes. Return to real scalars for the
remainder of the deck.
:::

---

### Additive inverses over $\mathbb{F}_2$ {#additive-inverses-over-f2}

An additive inverse adds to give $\vct{0}$; in $\mathbb{F}_2$, $1+1=0$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Find the additive inverse of $\vct{u}=[1,0,1,1]^{\mathsf T}$ in $\mathbb{F}_2^4$
<span class="exsub">Repeat for $\vct{w}=[0,1,1,0]^{\mathsf T}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Does the answer generalize to every vector in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$? Explain using XOR</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Both vectors are their own additive inverses. Use $\vct{u}$ on the board and
leave $\vct{w}$ and the generalization for students: each bit added to itself
by XOR gives zero, so $\vct{v}+\vct{v}=\vct{0}$ for every
$\vct{v}\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$.
:::

---

## Polynomials form a vector space {#polynomials-form-a-vector-space}

Write $\mathbb{P}_k$ for real polynomials in one variable $t$ of degree at
most $k$, including the zero polynomial

For example,

$$
\mathbb{P}_2=\{a_0+a_1t+a_2t^2:a_0,a_1,a_2\in\reals\}
$$

For $p,q\in\mathbb{P}_2$ and $c\in\reals$, use ordinary polynomial operations:

$$
(p+q)(t)=p(t)+q(t),
\qquad
(cp)(t)=c\,p(t)
$$

The zero vector is the zero polynomial

$$
0(t)=0
$$

::: {.key-point}
A polynomial is one vector; its coefficients provide one possible coordinate
description
:::

---

### Polynomials in several variables: total degree {#polynomials-in-several-variables-total-degree}

For integers $m\ge 0$ and $n\ge 1$, $\mathbb{P}_m(\reals^n)$ contains real
polynomials in $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ of [total degree at most $m$]{.alert}, including
the zero polynomial

A monomial's total degree is the sum of its exponents:

$$
x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_n^{\alpha_n}
\quad\text{has total degree}\quad
\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_n,
\qquad \alpha_j\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}
$$

A nonzero polynomial's total degree is the largest total degree of its
monomials with nonzero coefficients

$$
\mathbb{P}_2(\reals^2)
=\{a+bx+cy+dx^2+exy+fy^2:a,b,c,d,e,f\in\reals\}
$$

$x^2y\in\mathbb{P}_3(\reals^2)$, but $x^2y^2\notin\mathbb{P}_3(\reals^2)$

::: {.key-point}
$m$ bounds the total degree; $n$ counts the variables

Our one-variable notation is $\mathbb{P}_m=\mathbb{P}_m(\reals)$
:::

---

### Example: combine two-variable polynomials {#worked-example-combine-two-variable-polynomials}

In $\mathbb{P}_2(\reals^2)$, take

$$
p(x,y)=1+x+xy,
\qquad q(x,y)=2-y+x^2
$$

Combine matching monomials:

\begin{align*}
2p-q
&=2(1+x+xy)-(2-y+x^2)\\
&=2x+y-x^2+2xy
\end{align*}

Every remaining monomial has total degree at most two

::: {.key-point}
Addition and scalar multiplication change coefficients; they do not introduce
new monomials
:::

---

### Total degree and closure {#practice-total-degree-and-closure}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Work in $\mathbb{P}_2(\reals^2)$: each monomial's exponents sum to at most two
<span class="exsub">Which belong: $x^2+xy+y^2$, $x^2y$, $7$, and $0$?</span>
<span class="exsub">For $p=1+x+xy$ and $q=2-y+x^2$, compute $p+3q$</span>
<span class="exsub">Must the product of two members stay in this space? Give an example</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The first polynomial, 7, and 0 belong; x^2y has total degree three.
p+3q=7+x-3y+3x^2+xy. Multiplication need not preserve the space:
x^2 and y^2 belong but x^2y^2 does not. Closure under polynomial multiplication
is not a vector-space axiom.
:::

---

## Functions can be vectors {#functions-can-be-vectors}

Let $C[a,b]$ contain all continuous real-valued functions on $[a,b]$

$$
(f+g)(t)=f(t)+g(t),
\qquad
(cf)(t)=c\,f(t)
$$

The vector-space operations happen pointwise

$$
(2f-3g)(t)=2f(t)-3g(t)
$$

No finite list of functions can generate all of $C[a,b]$ by linear
combinations, for $a<b$

::: {.key-point}
A function is one vector, even though its values vary over an entire interval
:::

---

### Homogeneous linear DEs give vector spaces {#homogeneous-linear-des-give-vector-spaces}

The solutions of $f''+f=0$ on $\reals$ are functions

$$
f(t)=a\cos t+b\sin t,
\qquad a,b\in\reals
$$

For solutions $f,g$ and real constants $c,d$,

$$
(cf+dg)''+(cf+dg)=c(f''+f)+d(g''+g)=0
$$

The same closure holds for vector-valued solutions of
$\vct{y}'=\mat{A}\vct{y}$ with a fixed matrix $\mat{A}$

::: {.key-point}
Solutions of a homogeneous linear DE or system form a vector space of functions
:::

---

### Try another equation and a system {#try-another-equation-and-a-system}

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Test whether linear combinations of solutions are still solutions
<span class="exsub">For $h''-h=0$, verify that $e^t$ and $e^{-t}$ solve it and that every $ae^t+be^{-t}$ does too</span>
<span class="exsub">For $\mat{A}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, verify that $[e^t,0]^{\mathsf T}$ and $[0,e^{-t}]^{\mathsf T}$ solve $\vct{y}'=\mat{A}\vct{y}$ and so does every linear combination</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Use $f''+f=0$ on the previous slide as the board example. For the first
variant, both exponentials satisfy $h''=h$, and the differential operator is
linear. For the system, differentiate each displayed vector and multiply by
$\mat{A}$; both give the same result. Linearity then covers any combination.
The zero function solves both homogeneous equations. A nonhomogeneous equation
such as $h''-h=1$ does not have the zero function as a solution.
:::

---

### Nonhomogeneous DE solutions form an affine space {#nonhomogeneous-de-solutions-form-an-affine-space}

For $h''-h=1$, the constant function $h_p=-1$ is one solution

The solutions of $z''-z=0$ are $z=ae^t+be^{-t}$, so every solution is

$$
h(t)=-1+ae^t+be^{-t},
\qquad a,b\in\reals
$$

The zero function does not solve $h''-h=1$

::: {.key-point}
When a nonhomogeneous linear DE has a solution, its solution set is a
particular solution plus the homogeneous solution space
:::

---

### Affine solution spaces {#practice-affine-solution-spaces}

Use one particular solution plus the homogeneous solutions

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Find one particular solution and describe the full solution set
<span class="exsub">$g''+g=2$</span>
<span class="exsub">$y'-y=3$</span>
</span>
:::

The corresponding homogeneous solutions are $a\cos t+b\sin t$ and $ce^t$,
respectively

For each set, explain why it is not a vector space under the usual operations

::: {.notes}
For $g''+g=2$, use the particular solution $g_p=2$. All solutions are
$g(t)=2+a\cos t+b\sin t$. For $y'-y=3$, use $y_p=-3$. All solutions are
$y(t)=-3+ce^t$. In each case the zero function fails the equation, so the
solution set is affine rather than a vector space.
:::

---

### Finite Fourier sums are vectors {#finite-fourier-sums-are-vectors}

Use $\sqrt{-1}$ for the imaginary unit, leaving $i$ available as an index

On $[0,1]$, use the Fourier modes

$$
\phi_k(t)=e^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}\,kt},
\qquad k\in\mathbb{Z},
\qquad \phi_k(t+1)=\phi_k(t)
$$

Start with their finite sums over complex scalars:

$$
\mathcal{T}
=\left\{\sum_{k=-N}^{N}c_k\phi_k:N=0,1,2,\ldots,\ c_k\in\mathbb{C}\right\}
$$

Each vector in $\mathcal{T}$ is a complex-valued function on $[0,1]$ with a
1-periodic extension

Adding two finite sums or scaling by a complex number stays in $\mathcal{T}$

::: {.key-point}
Complex exponentials are vectors; finite Fourier sums form a vector space
:::

::: {.notes}
Full Fourier series may involve infinitely many terms. To include their
limits, choose a function space and a notion of convergence; this goes beyond
the finite linear combinations used in this deck.
:::

## Affine sets usually fail the zero-vector test {#affine-sets-usually-fail-the-zero-vector-test}

Under ordinary operations, the zero vector is $[0,0]^{\mathsf T}$

$$
L=\left\{
\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}
+t\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}:t\in\reals
\right\}
$$

This line does not contain $\vct{0}$, so it cannot be a vector space under the
usual operations

Its direction set

$$
W=\left\{t\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix}:t\in\reals\right\}
$$

is a vector space

::: {.key-point}
An affine set is a point plus a direction subspace

It is itself a subspace exactly when it contains the origin
:::

## The operations are part of the definition {#the-operations-are-part-of-the-definition}

On $V=\{(x,y):x,y\in\reals\}$, suppose

$$
(x,y)\mathbin{\boxplus}(u,v)=(x+u-1,y+v-1)
$$

The usual pair $(0,0)$ is not the zero vector for this addition

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Find the element $\vct{z}$ satisfying $(x,y)\mathbin{\boxplus}\vct{z}=(x,y)$ for every $(x,y)$
<span class="exsub">Why must scalar multiplication also be specified before deciding whether these operations define a vector space?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The additive identity is $(1,1)$. The point is not to finish constructing an
unusual vector space, but to establish that the underlying set alone does not
determine its vector-space structure.
:::

# Subspaces and Span

- [A subspace inherits its operations](#a-subspace-inherits-its-operations)
- [One combined test proves the subspace properties](#one-combined-test-proves-the-subspace-properties)
- [The zero vector is the quickest rejection test](#the-zero-vector-is-the-quickest-rejection-test)
- [Upper-triangular matrices form a subspace](#upper-triangular-matrices-form-a-subspace)
- [Homogeneous systems produce subspaces](#homogeneous-systems-produce-subspaces)

The [companion notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH332Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/demonstrations/06-general-vector-spaces.ipynb)
explores polynomial constraints, closure, and affine sets

## A subspace inherits its operations {#a-subspace-inherits-its-operations}

A subset $W\subseteq V$ is a [subspace]{.alert} when $W$ is itself a vector space
using the addition and scalar multiplication already defined on $V$

Examples in $\reals^n$ for $n\ge 2$:

- any line through the origin
- any plane through the origin when $n\ge 3$
- $\{\vct{0}\}$ and $\reals^n$

Examples in $\mathbb{P}_3$ (polynomials in $t$ of degree at most three):

- polynomials of degree at most two
- polynomials satisfying $p(1)=0$

::: {.key-point}
A subspace uses the same operations as its ambient space
:::

## One combined test proves the subspace properties {#one-combined-test-proves-the-subspace-properties}

A nonempty subset $W\subseteq V$ is a subspace if

$$
c\vct{u}+d\vct{v}\in W
$$

for every $\vct{u},\vct{v}\in W$ and every $c,d\in\reals$

This one condition gives

- closure under addition by taking $c=d=1$
- closure under scalar multiplication by taking $d=0$
- the zero vector by taking $c=d=0$
- additive inverses by taking $c=-1$ and $d=0$

::: {.key-point}
Subspaces are exactly the subsets closed under linear combinations
:::

## The zero vector is the quickest rejection test {#the-zero-vector-is-the-quickest-rejection-test}

For each subset of $\reals^2$, ask first whether $\vct{0}$ belongs

$$
W_1=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}:x+2y=0\right\}
$$

$$
W_2=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}:x+2y=1\right\}
$$

$W_1$ passes the zero test and is closed under linear combinations

$W_2$ fails immediately because $\vct{0}\notin W_2$

::: {.key-point}
Homogeneous linear conditions define subspaces; shifted conditions usually
define affine sets
:::

---

### Containing zero is necessary, not sufficient {#containing-zero-is-necessary-not-sufficient}

The union of the coordinate axes contains the origin

$$
W=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}:xy=0\right\}
$$

Every scalar multiple of a vector in $W$ stays on its axis

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Does $W$ form a subspace of $\reals^2$?
<span class="exsub">Choose one nonzero vector on each axis</span>
<span class="exsub">Does their sum belong to $W$?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.key-point}
The zero-vector test can reject a set; closure is still needed to accept it
:::

::: {.notes}
Take [1,0]^T and [0,1]^T. Their sum [1,1]^T is off both axes, so W is not
closed under addition. Containing zero and being closed under scalar
multiplication together are still insufficient. This is a necessary-versus-
sufficient-condition example, not a new subspace test.
:::

## Upper-triangular matrices form a subspace {#upper-triangular-matrices-form-a-subspace}

Recall the [matrix families in {{< meta decks.d03.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#triangular-matrices-expose-pivots)

Use ordinary matrix addition and real scalar multiplication in $\reals^{n\times n}$

The upper-triangular matrices satisfy

$$
U=\{\mat{A}\in\reals^{n\times n}:a_{ij}=0\text{ whenever }i>j\}
$$

For $n=3$, their form is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a&b&c\\0&d&e\\0&0&f\end{bmatrix},
\qquad a,b,c,d,e,f\in\reals
$$

The zero matrix belongs to $U$; for $\mat{A},\mat{B}\in U$ and $r,s\in\reals$,

$$
(r\mat{A}+s\mat{B})_{ij}=ra_{ij}+sb_{ij}=0\qquad(i>j)
$$

::: {.key-point}
Upper-triangular matrices form a vector space: linear combinations preserve
the zeros below the diagonal
:::

---

### Permutation matrices do not form a subspace {#permutation-matrices-do-not-form-a-subspace}

For fixed $n\ge1$, a permutation matrix has exactly one $1$ in each row and
column and $0$ everywhere else

In $\reals^{2\times2}$, the only permutation matrices are

$$
\mat{I}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mat{P}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}
$$

The zero matrix is not a permutation matrix

Addition and scalar multiplication also fail closure:

$$
\mat{I}+\mat{P}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
2\mat{I}=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Permutation matrices are closed under matrix multiplication, but fail the
vector-space tests for addition and scalar multiplication
:::

---

### Which other matrix families are subspaces? {#which-other-matrix-families-are-subspaces}

Use ordinary addition and real scalar multiplication in $\reals^{n\times n}$,
with fixed $n\ge2$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Decide whether each family is a subspace
<span class="exsub">Diagonal matrices: $a_{ij}=0$ when $i\ne j$</span>
<span class="exsub">Lower-triangular matrices: $a_{ij}=0$ when $i<j$</span>
<span class="exsub">Symmetric matrices: $\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}=\mat{A}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Tridiagonal matrices: $a_{ij}=0$ when $|i-j|>1$</span>
<span class="exsub">Invertible matrices: a matrix inverse exists</span>
<span class="exsub">Orthogonal matrices: $\mat{A}^{\mathsf T}\mat{A}=\mat{I}$</span>
</span>
:::

For each yes, prove closure under linear combinations; for each no, give a
failed test or counterexample

::: {.notes}
Diagonal, lower-triangular, and tridiagonal matrices contain the zero matrix
and preserve their required zero entries under linear combinations. Symmetric
matrices contain zero and satisfy $(rA+sB)^{\mathsf T}=rA+sB$ when A and B
are symmetric. Invertible and orthogonal matrices exclude zero; I belongs
to each family, while 0I and I+(-I) do not. Matrix multiplication is not a
vector-space operation. These are subspaces of a fixed-size matrix space;
do not mix matrix sizes.
:::

## Homogeneous systems produce subspaces {#homogeneous-systems-produce-subspaces}

The [null space]{.alert} of an $m\times n$ matrix $\mat{A}$ is

$$
\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})
=\{\vct{x}\in\reals^n:\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{0}\}
$$

If $\vct{x},\vct{y}\in\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})$, then

$$
\mat{A}(c\vct{x}+d\vct{y})
=c\mat{A}\vct{x}+d\mat{A}\vct{y}
=\vct{0}
$$

If $\mat{A}\vct{x}_p=\vct{b}$, the full solution set is
$\vct{x}_p+\operatorname{null}(\mat{A})$

For $\vct{b}\ne\vct{0}$, this affine set does not contain the zero vector

This gives a name to the homogeneous solutions found by
[elimination in {{< meta decks.d01.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#read-the-solution-set)

::: {.key-point}
The null space records every input direction that a matrix sends to zero
:::

# Spans and Membership

- [Span is the subspace generated by chosen vectors](#span-is-the-subspace-generated-by-chosen-vectors)
- [In $\reals^n$, span is matrix–vector multiplication](#in-rn-span-is-matrix-vector-multiplication)
- [Spanning polynomials means matching every coefficient](#spanning-polynomials-means-matching-every-coefficient)
- [Example: a polynomial subspace](#worked-example-a-polynomial-subspace)
- [A subspace question becomes a closure question](#a-subspace-question-becomes-a-closure-question)

## Span is the subspace generated by chosen vectors {#span-is-the-subspace-generated-by-chosen-vectors}

For vectors $\vct{v}_1,\ldots,\vct{v}_k$ in a real vector space $V$,

$$
\operatorname{span}\{\vct{v}_1,\ldots,\vct{v}_k\}
=\left\{c_1\vct{v}_1+\cdots+c_k\vct{v}_k:c_i\in\reals\right\}
$$

The span

- contains the chosen vectors
- contains every linear combination of them
- is the smallest subspace containing them

::: {.key-point}
Span answers a reachability question: which vectors can these generators
build?
:::

---

## In $\reals^n$, span is matrix–vector multiplication {#in-rn-span-is-matrix-vector-multiplication}

For $\vct{v}_j\in\reals^n$, collect the chosen vectors as columns:

$$
\mat{V}=\begin{bmatrix}\vct{v}_1&\cdots&\vct{v}_k\end{bmatrix}\in\reals^{n\times k},
\qquad
\vct{c}=\begin{bmatrix}c_1&\cdots&c_k\end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}\in\reals^k
$$

$$
\operatorname{span}\{\vct{v}_1,\ldots,\vct{v}_k\}
=\{\mat{V}\vct{c}:\vct{c}\in\reals^k\},
\qquad
\mat{V}\vct{c}=\sum_{j=1}^k c_j\vct{v}_j
$$

This is [matrix–vector multiplication in {{< meta decks.d01.short_title >}}]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#what-ax-means-by-columns)

::: {.key-point}
The span is the set of all outputs $\mat{V}\vct{c}$ as the coefficient vector
$\vct{c}$ varies
:::

---

### Example: a span is a plane {#worked-example-a-span-is-a-plane}

Take $\vct{v}_1=[1,0,1]^{\mathsf T}$ and
$\vct{v}_2=[0,1,1]^{\mathsf T}$

$$
\mat{V}\vct{c}
=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}c_1\\c_2\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}c_1\\c_2\\c_1+c_2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Thus

$$
\operatorname{span}\{\vct{v}_1,\vct{v}_2\}
=\{[x,y,z]^{\mathsf T}:z=x+y\}
$$

For example, $[2,-1,1]^{\mathsf T}=2\vct{v}_1-\vct{v}_2$ belongs;
$[0,0,1]^{\mathsf T}$ does not

::: {.key-point}
A spanning description and an equation can describe the same subspace
:::

---

### Membership and an extra generator {#practice-membership-and-an-extra-generator}

Keep $\vct{v}_1=[1,0,1]^{\mathsf T}$ and
$\vct{v}_2=[0,1,1]^{\mathsf T}$; let
$\vct{v}_3=[1,1,2]^{\mathsf T}$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Use coefficients or the plane equation $z=x+y$
<span class="exsub">Is $[3,2,5]^{\mathsf T}$ in the span? Find coefficients</span>
<span class="exsub">Is $[3,2,4]^{\mathsf T}$ in the span?</span>
<span class="exsub">Does adding $\vct{v}_3$ enlarge the span? Explain</span>
<span class="exsub">Find two different coefficient lists in $\vct{v}_3=c_1\vct{v}_1+c_2\vct{v}_2+c_3\vct{v}_3$; zero coefficients are allowed</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
[3,2,5]^T=3v_1+2v_2; [3,2,4]^T fails z=x+y. Since v_3=v_1+v_2,
adding it does not enlarge the span. For part (d), the list [1,1,0]^T means
v_3=1v_1+1v_2+0v_3, whereas [0,0,1]^T means v_3=0v_1+0v_2+1v_3.
The three coefficient positions correspond to the ordered generators
(v_1,v_2,v_3); using this list does not require every coefficient to be
nonzero. More generally [1-s,1-s,s]^T represents v_3 for every real s.
The target vector stays the same while its coefficients change because the
generators are dependent. Call these coefficient lists, not coordinates in
a basis: a basis would give a unique list.
:::

## Spanning polynomials means matching every coefficient {#spanning-polynomials-means-matching-every-coefficient}

Let

$$
p_1(t)=1+t,
\qquad
p_2(t)=t+t^2,
\qquad
p_3(t)=1-t^2
$$

To span $\mathbb{P}_2$, the equation must be solvable for every real
$a_0,a_1,a_2$

$$
c_1p_1+c_2p_2+c_3p_3=a_0+a_1t+a_2t^2
$$

Matching coefficients gives $\mat{A}\vct{c}=\vct{a}$:

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&1\\
1&1&0\\
0&1&-1
\end{bmatrix}}_{\mat{A}}
\begin{bmatrix}c_1\\c_2\\c_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}a_0\\a_1\\a_2\end{bmatrix}
$$

---

### A singular coefficient matrix cannot reach every polynomial {#a-singular-coefficient-matrix-cannot-reach-every-polynomial}

Keep $p_1=1+t$, $p_2=t+t^2$, and $p_3=1-t^2$

The columns of $\mat{A}$ collect their coefficients of $1,t,t^2$, so

$$
\vct{A}_3=\vct{A}_1-\vct{A}_2
\quad\implies\quad
\det(\mat{A})=0
$$

Thus $\mat{A}$ is [singular]{.alert}: $\mat{A}\vct{c}=\vct{a}$ cannot be solved
for every coefficient vector $\vct{a}\in\reals^3$

The same relation holds between the polynomials:

$$
p_3=p_1-p_2
$$

In every resulting $a_0+a_1t+a_2t^2$, $a_1=a_0+a_2$

The constant polynomial $1$ has $(a_0,a_1,a_2)=(1,0,0)$ and fails this condition

::: {.key-point}
These three polynomials do not span $\mathbb{P}_2$: their singular coefficient
matrix cannot produce every coefficient vector
:::

---

### Membership in a polynomial span {#practice-membership-in-a-polynomial-span}

Keep $p_1=1+t$ and $p_2=t+t^2$, and let
$W=\operatorname{span}\{p_1,p_2\}$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Test membership by solving $c_1p_1+c_2p_2=p$ for real $c_1,c_2$
<span class="exsub">Write $2+3t+t^2$ as a combination of $p_1,p_2$, if possible</span>
<span class="exsub">Decide whether $1$ belongs to $W$</span>
<span class="exsub">Give a coefficient test for $a_0+a_1t+a_2t^2$ to belong to $W$</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
$2+3t+t^2=2p_1+p_2$. The constant polynomial $1$ is not in $W$ because
every combination $c_1p_1+c_2p_2$ has coefficients
$(a_0,a_1,a_2)=(c_1,c_1+c_2,c_2)$. Thus membership is equivalent to
$a_1=a_0+a_2$.
:::

---

## Example: a polynomial subspace {#worked-example-a-polynomial-subspace}

In $\mathbb{P}_3$ (degree at most three), consider $U=\{p:p(0)=0\}$

The zero polynomial lies in $U$; for $p,q\in U$ and $c,d\in\reals$,

$$
(cp+dq)(0)=cp(0)+dq(0)=0
$$

Also, $p(t)=a_1t+a_2t^2+a_3t^3$, so

$$
U=\operatorname{span}\{t,t^2,t^3\}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Use the defining condition to prove closure, then use coefficients to find a
spanning set
:::


## A subspace question becomes a closure question {#a-subspace-question-becomes-a-closure-question}

Let

$$
W=\{p\in\mathbb{P}_3:p(1)=0\}
$$

::: {.exitem}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Show that $W$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{P}_3$
<span class="exsub">Start with $p,q\in W$ and $c,d\in\reals$</span>
<span class="exsub">Evaluate $(cp+dq)(1)$</span>
<span class="exsub">Find three polynomials that span $W$</span>
<span class="exsub">Can fewer than three polynomials span $W$? Why?</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Since $p(1)=q(1)=0$, $(cp+dq)(1)=0$. Every polynomial in $W$ factors as
$(t-1)(a+bt+ct^2)$, so one spanning set is
$\{t-1,t(t-1),t^2(t-1)\}$. The coefficients $(a,b,c)$ range over all of
$\reals^3$; two chosen polynomials yield at most two coefficient columns and
cannot span that three-dimensional coefficient space. Thus no set of fewer
than three polynomials spans $W$.
:::

---

### More subspace tests with functions {#more-subspace-tests-with-functions}

Use continuous real-valued functions on $[0,1]$, with pointwise addition and
real scalar multiplication

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Which sets are subspaces of $C[0,1]$?
<span class="exsub">$W_0=\{f:f(0)=0\}$</span>
<span class="exsub">$W_1=\{f:f(0)=1\}$</span>
<span class="exsub">$W_2=\{f:f(0)=f(1)\}$</span>
</span>
:::

Check the zero function and closure under $cf+dg$

::: {.notes}
The polynomial example supplies the board model. $W_0$ and $W_2$ are
subspaces because their defining conditions are homogeneous and preserved by
linear combinations. $W_1$ is not: the zero function does not belong to it.
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- A vector space has addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the axioms
- Polynomials, matrices, and functions can be vectors
- A subspace inherits the operations and is closed under linear combinations
- The span is the smallest subspace containing its generators
- A subspace can be described by generators or homogeneous linear constraints
